paras: The threatened lynching of Henry Lawson took place in Chattanooga, Tennessee, in July 1881, when a mob gathered at night in front of the jail where Lawson, a Black man accused of raping and cutting a young woman, was being held. According to a Chattanooga telegram dated July 11, the men were deterred by a strong sheriff's guard. Lawson was later convicted in the circuit court at Chattanooga and sentenced to hang, and the case ran as brief items in Georgia, Tennessee and Louisiana papers.

The accusation first appeared in the Chattanooga Times, whose account, as relayed by the Savannah Morning News on July 9, said that Miss Nancy Donaldson, 17, had been raped and "horribly mutilated with a razor" on Missionary Ridge a few days earlier. The item named the accused as "a mulatto demon named Henry Lawson, who had a wife and five children," and said he had been pursued, captured and jailed to await trial. Later Tennessee reports dated the offense to July 4 and placed it in Hamilton County, near Chattanooga.

A telegram from Chattanooga dated July 11 reported that "a negro name Hugh Lawson," accused of raping a young lady the week before and mutilating her body, had been arrested and lodged in jail. It said there was "great danger of his being lynched" and that a mob had gathered in front of the jail the previous night for that purpose. A strong sheriff's guard deterred the crowd, though the dispatch added that excitement was still high. The telegram gave no size for the mob, named none of its members and reported no shots or injuries.

Lawson was tried in the circuit court at Chattanooga in the last week of July. On July 28 the Knoxville Daily Chronicle reported that on the previous Tuesday the jury had returned a verdict of guilty "without extenuating circumstances" and fixed the punishment at hanging, with the judge to pass sentence and set the date the next day. Later reports disagreed about whether an appeal was taken and on which Friday he was to be hanged. No report of the execution, of an appeal's outcome or of any further move against the jail appears in the coverage, which ends with a Cleveland, Tennessee, notice of August 5.

The jail mob is known from a single telegram, which the Louisiana Capitolian of Baton Rouge printed among its "Telegraphic News" on July 14 and again on July 16. The Chattanooga Times account of the assault reached Georgia readers in identical wording through the Savannah Morning News's "Georgia Affairs" column on July 9 and the Marietta Journal on July 14. None of these items mentioned the mob, and the telegram stated the rape as fact.

Tennessee weeklies carried the trial in a sentence or two, the Knoxville Daily Chronicle under the headline "Death Sentence for Rape" and the Morristown Gazette in nearly the same words on August 3. Their language for Lawson ran from "the black fiend" in Knoxville and Morristown to "the regro rapist and murderer" in the Cleveland Weekly Herald, while the Winchester Home Journal wrote more plainly of "Henry Lawson, col." and "a nameless crime."

The telegram called the accused "Hugh Lawson," while the Chattanooga Times account and every trial report name him Henry Lawson, the better-supported form since it traces to the local paper and the court. The Knoxville Daily Chronicle said an appeal would be taken and the Morristown Gazette that one was taken, but the Winchester Home Journal said "No appeal was prayed." The Home Journal set the hanging for Friday, August 26, whereas the Cleveland Weekly Herald gave Friday, September 2. Only the Weekly Herald called Lawson a "murderer"; the other reports describe rape and mutilation and do not say that the young woman died.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Lawson
bases: A mob gathered at the Chattanooga jail to lynch a jailed Black man accused of rape and was turned back by the sheriff's guard (A2, A4); he was later tried and sentenced to hang (A5, A7).

The mob that gathered to lynch Lawson for an alleged rape was deterred by the sheriff's guard and no one was killed (A4); he was afterwards convicted and sentenced by a court (A5, A7), so this was a threatened lynching, not a lynching.
The jail mob appears only in one Chattanooga telegram, printed twice by the same Baton Rouge paper (A2, A4); the accusation, arrest and later conviction are reported independently (A1, A5, A7).

framing.detail: The Baton Rouge telegram reported the jail mob flatly among other crime items, stating the rape as fact and the lynching danger without comment.
Georgia papers relaying the Chattanooga Times called the assault 'a horrible tale' and Lawson 'a mulatto demon', while noting he was held for trial.
Tennessee papers reported the conviction under 'Death Sentence for Rape' and called Lawson 'the black fiend' and 'the regro rapist and murderer'.
